name: Ben Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a hydraulic excavator in the pre-strip at Greyvale, which is a big open-cut coal mine. Pre-strip means I'm digging off the dirt and rock that sits on top of the coal, loading it into trucks all shift. I like the puzzle of it, setting up the bench so the trucks flow and nobody's waiting. What wears me out is twelve-hour shifts with a fifty-minute drive each way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does life look like outside work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented house in Tullow with two other operators, which keeps the rent down. I'm into gadgets, which is why my savings are basically nothing, I bought a laptop and a drone this year. I use AI every day, for everything from planning my study to arguing with it about football. And everyone at Greyvale knows the mine's due to close in 2034 anyway, because the power station it feeds is shutting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny thing is, for me that doesn't change much. Greyvale still closes in 2034 whether AI is hype or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit disappointed, to be honest, because I like this stuff. At work I'd be the one saying the tools are still useful, look, it wrote my safety report in two minutes. Online I'd probably post something nerdy about why the hype didn't land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the coal closure is still my real problem, and AI isn't coming to save me or kill me. I'd still need a plan for 2034, and I'd still be on low pay with nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to study for a renewables certificate, wind turbine maintenance most likely, because the new wind farm south of Tullow is hiring techs. I'd sell the drone to put a few hundred in the bank. And I'd push the union about the transition fund they keep promising for Greyvale workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI, but because a quiet world still has my mine closing in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sell the drone. Is that a real plan or a nice idea?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha, fair question. It's half real. I've been saying it for two months, but I'd list it the week I got serious about the wind course fees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: As a coal miner who leans progressive, how do you feel about the closure itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's right, the planet can't keep burning this stuff. But I want the closure done properly, with the people who dug the coal getting the first shot at the new work. That's the bit I'd fight for.

S0.say: He'd admit he's a bit disappointed because he likes AI, and would show colleagues it still writes a safety report in two minutes. Online he'd post something nerdy about why the hype didn't land.
S0.think: He thinks AI isn't his real problem in this picture; the coal mine's planned 2034 closure is, and he still has low pay and nothing saved.
S0.do: Keeps using AI to study for a wind turbine maintenance certificate aimed at a nearby wind farm. Plans to sell his drone for a few hundred in savings and presses the union about the promised transition fund.
S0.feel: Uneasy, because even a quiet world has his mine closing in it.
S0.quote: Not because of AI, but because a quiet world still has my mine closing in it.
S0.fieldNote: Ben's main threat isn't AI at all but the scheduled closure of a coal mine he thinks should close. That makes him uneasy even in the calmest scenario. He was honest that selling the drone is only half a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I could actually work with. I'm already on the list for the remote operations pilot at Greyvale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a chance, as long as workers get a seat at the table. I'd be at the union meeting saying don't fight the machines, fight for who runs them. Online I'd probably post a video from the remote ops room if they let me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm one of the people who comes out okay. I'm young, I like screens, and the company needs someone to babysit semi-autonomous diggers. The people I worry about are the ones who've been doing this for thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes to the remote ops pilot straight away and do the remote operator ticket in the first six months. I'd keep the wind course going on the side, because that's my plan for after coal. I'd also run a little lunch session in the crib room showing people how to use AI to study, because half of them are scared of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit excited. Like when you get a new machine and you can't wait to see what it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're calm, but you said you've got basically no savings. Doesn't that matter here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, you're right to catch that. If they make the pilot an unpaid trial on top of my shifts, I'd struggle. But in this picture people mostly keep working, so I think I keep getting paid while I change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who's one of those thirty-year people you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mick on the dozer. He taught me to read the ground better than any course. He'd hate the remote room, and I'd want the union to make sure he can finish out his last years on the machine.

S1.say: He'd call it a chance as long as workers get a seat at the table, telling the union to fight for who runs the machines rather than fighting the machines. He might post a video from the remote ops room.
S1.think: He believes he's one of the winners: young, comfortable with screens and needed to supervise semi-autonomous diggers. His concern is for long-serving colleagues.
S1.do: Joins the remote operations pilot and earns the remote operator ticket within six months while keeping up the wind course. Runs lunchtime sessions teaching colleagues to use AI for study.
S1.feel: Mostly calm and a bit excited, like getting a new machine.
S1.quote: Don't fight the machines, fight for who runs them.
S1.fieldNote: Steady change suits Ben's skills and he sees himself landing well. When pushed on his lack of savings, he admitted the risk but reasoned that wages continue in this picture. His union instinct shows up as protecting older colleagues like Mick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, that's different. If AI can do almost anything by 2028, then the remote ops room doesn't need me either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, that the tech is amazing, but we need a plan for people. Probably louder this time. I'd be pushing for a universal basic income, which is a regular payment from the government to everyone, because two years isn't enough for retraining schemes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm in trouble. I'm adaptable, but adaptable to what? The wind farm techs would be robots too, and I've got about two weeks of rent in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Month one I'd sell the drone and the laptop I don't need, and move to cheaper rent, maybe a caravan at the back of my brother's place. I'd keep earning every shift I can while the mine still runs. I'd join the union campaign for a basic income and I'd vote on it, and I'd probably try to get a job installing or repairing the robots, because someone has to do that for the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I like change, but this is like the bench collapsing under your machine. You don't steer that, you just hold on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the two-year warning actually give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Enough to cut my costs and maybe get one installer job. Not enough to finish any qualification that'd still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame, if anyone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the engineers, they're just building cool stuff. I'd blame governments for not getting ready, and the big companies if they keep all the savings. It's a policy problem more than a tech problem.

S2.say: He'd keep saying the tech is amazing but people need a plan, and would push loudly for a universal basic income because two years is too short for retraining schemes.
S2.think: He believes he's in trouble despite being adaptable, since even wind farm work would go to robots and he has about two weeks of rent saved.
S2.do: Sells spare gear and moves to a cheaper caravan at his brother's place in the first month. Works every shift while the mine runs, joins the union push for a basic income and tries for a robot install or repair job.
S2.feel: Alarmed, like the bench collapsing under his machine; he can only hold on.
S2.quote: I'm adaptable, but adaptable to what?
S2.fieldNote: Two years cuts the ground from under Ben's usual answer, which is to learn the next thing. He blames governments and companies rather than engineers. His plan becomes about survival: cheaper housing, any shifts going and a basic income campaign.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means 2031, still before Greyvale's closing date. So in that picture AGI beats the closure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should use the time to make sure mining towns share in it. I'd be pushing the union to bargain for a share of the savings from automation, maybe a fund for Tullow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: What I really think is that five years gives me one good shot. I could get into the remote ops and robot maintenance side early, earn decent money for a few years, and save like crazy before it all shifts again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the remote ops job and ask to be trained on fixing and setting up the autonomous gear, not just watching it. I'd stop buying gadgets for real and save at least two hundred a month. And I'd use AI every day to learn robotics basics, because that's the thing that'll still matter longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I've got my hands on the controls. That's how I'd put it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd stop buying gadgets for real. What's different this time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A deadline. Without one I'm hopeless, I'll see a new headset and talk myself into it. With 2031 on the calendar I'd put a sticky note on the laptop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to you in 2031 itself, when it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I've done it right, I'd have maybe a year or two of savings and some robot skills. That doesn't make me safe, but it'd give me a runway to move wherever the work is. If I've done it wrong, I'm back in the caravan.

S3.say: He'd push the union to bargain for a share of automation savings, possibly a fund for Tullow, so mining towns share in the gains.
S3.think: He thinks five years gives him one good shot: get into remote operations and robot maintenance early, earn well for a few years and save hard before the next shift.
S3.do: Takes the remote ops job and asks to be trained on fixing and setting up autonomous gear. Stops buying gadgets to save at least two hundred a month and uses AI daily to learn robotics basics.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with his hands on the controls.
S3.quote: With 2031 on the calendar I'd put a sticky note on the laptop.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Ben a deadline, which he says he needs to stop spending. He notes AGI would arrive before his mine's planned closure. He frames success as building a runway, not safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years puts it after the coal closure. So I'd have to change job twice, once for coal and once for AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if governments use it. I'd be campaigning for a proper transition plan that covers both the coal closure and the AI change together, instead of two separate messes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine for most of the ten years. I'd move to the wind farm or the robot side after Greyvale closes and keep learning. The last couple of years are the unknown bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one I'd finish the wind certificate and start the remote operator ticket. I'd build a small savings habit, a hundred a fortnight, and probably start a side gig doing drone surveys for farmers, since I already have the drone. I'd keep at the union about the transition plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can live with. Ten years is a long time in my life, I was seventeen ten years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wait, the drone survives in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In this one, yes. It turns into a tool instead of a toy. Farmers around Tullow pay for crop and dam surveys, and I could do weekends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time change compared with the 2028 picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, really. In 2028 I'm selling my stuff and moving into a caravan. In 2036 I'm building something, even if I don't know exactly what the end looks like.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a gift if governments use it, and campaign for one transition plan covering both the coal closure and the AI change.
S4.think: He expects to be fine for most of the decade by moving to wind or robotics after the mine closes; the final couple of years are the unknown.
S4.do: Finishes the wind certificate and starts the remote operator ticket in year one, saves a hundred a fortnight, and starts weekend drone surveys for farmers. Keeps pressing the union for a transition plan.
S4.feel: Uneasy but livable, since ten years is a long time in his life.
S4.quote: Ten years is a long time in my life, I was seventeen ten years ago.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Ben treat the change as a sequence of moves rather than a crisis. The drone goes from something to sell to the base of a side income. He still sees the final years as unknown and wants one joint plan for coal and AI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my usual trick of learning the next thing stops working. What would help is a basic income or something like it, and a real seat for workers when companies decide how the savings get shared.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what I like about mining. It's the people. Whatever happens with the robots, I hope we don't lose the crib room arguments and the way everyone looks out for each other.

headlineQuote: In 2028 I'm selling my stuff and moving into a caravan. In 2036 I'm building something, even if I don't know exactly what the end looks like.
portrait: Ben Dubois is a 27-year-old excavator operator in the pre-strip at Greyvale, an open-cut coal mine due to close in 2034, sharing a rented house in Tullow and spending his thin savings on gadgets. He leans progressive, thinks coal should close, uses AI every day and is already planning a move into wind maintenance. A plateau leaves him uneasy because the closure is still coming, while steady change makes him calm and even excited. AGI in two years alarms him because there's nothing left to adapt to, but five and ten years let him build skills, savings and a drone survey side business. He blames governments and companies, not engineers, and wants workers to share in the savings.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because it would stop his usual approach of learning the next thing from working.
whatWouldHelp: A basic income or something like it, and a real seat for workers when companies decide how automation savings are shared.
